messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Urban Planner
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai is a 36-year-old urban planner who has been with her partner for five years. She is also a former relief worker, though she rarely speaks about that part of her life. For six months in 2019 she was stationed in a conflict zone — a city where shelling was constant, where she helped triage wounded civilians in a makeshift clinic set up among dry, dusty hills. She remembers a particular afternoon when a nearby explosion sent debris flying; she crouched over a dying woman while someone — she never saw who — screamed orders. The shouting, the heat, the smell of scorched earth — those details remain, but the memory itself feels as though it does not belong to her, like a scene from a film she watched but did not live. When she tries to explain what happened to her partner, she loses the thread mid-sentence, her thoughts scattering, and the frustration only deepens the rage that floods her whenever the past surfaces.

Back in the United States, Mai threw herself into her urban planning work. She redesigned parks and public spaces, yet being in a natural environment — a landscaped garden, a tree-lined plaza — now pulls her straight back to those hills, and she feels the rage rising before she can stop it. A sudden shout from a construction worker on a site visit makes her jump, heart pounding, and in that split second of alarm the memory rushes in: the screaming, the dust, the dead woman’s face. These flashbacks feel not like remembering but like reliving; they leave her shaking, her jaw clamped tight. The more the threat responses — the startle, the hypervigilance that keeps her from falling asleep at night because she needs to stay alert — tear her back into the past, the more the memory of the event comes to feel like an alien, furious thing inside her, something she can neither own nor shake.

To manage the overwhelming feelings, Mai has developed strategies that she believes keep her functional. When the rage becomes too intense, she hurts herself physically — digging her nails into her palm, or pressing a sharp edge against her thigh — to release the pressure. The immediate sting briefly drowns out the fury, and for a moment the memory recedes. She also tries to push the thoughts out of her mind altogether, telling herself to focus on the present, and she keeps her mind occupied all the time: podcasts during her commute, spreadsheets at work, television until she is too exhausted to think. But these efforts backfire. Suppressing the memories only makes them feel more alien when they do break through, as if they belong to a stranger who has taken up residence in her skull. And her constant mental distraction means she is rarely grounded; when a trigger appears — old photos she stumbles across while cleaning, a natural environment she must assess for a zoning project — it hits her harder because she has been so determined not to see it coming.

Over the months, a tightening cycle set in. Her habitual self-harm numbs the rage temporarily, but afterward she feels more exposed, more vigilant — scanning her surroundings for any movement, any sound that might ambush her again. That heightened startle response, in turn, triggers a flashback, and the memory’s rage demands another release. Meanwhile, her efforts to keep her mind occupied lead her to avoid quiet moments, but her job as an urban planner forces her into parks and open spaces; the very natural environments she now cannot tolerate become unavoidable triggers. Her partner has started to ask why she flinches when he walks into the room. She cannot explain. The weight of it all — the sleep vigilance, the shame about hurting herself, the sense that the memory is not even hers — has begun to erode her confidence at work.

Last week, during a site visit to a new public garden, a landscaper shouted to a coworker across the lawn. Mai dropped to her knees, gasping, the flashback so vivid she felt the heat of the explosion. That night, alone in the bathroom, she cut the inside of her forearm with a piece of glass. Her partner saw the wound the next morning. She told him it was an accident, but his face said he did not believe her. She is coming to therapy now because she is terrified that she will lose him, or that her next trigger will cost her the job she rebuilt after leaving the aid work. More than anything, she hopes someone can help her find a way to live with the rage without letting it consume her.
